items.prompt: White to move. A different move order, the same pawn structure. Tap every black pawn on the wing where Black has the majority (files a to d).

hints: Count the pawns of each colour on files a to d.
White has a2, b2 and d4 there. Black has more.
Black's four are on a7, b7, c6 and d5.
items.explain: On files a to d White has a2, b2, d4 (three) and Black has a7, b7, c6, d5 (four), so the majority there is Black's. On files e to h White has four against three. The structure is the same as in the first position; only the move order differs.

items.prompt: White to move, after the trades in the model. Tap the black pawn that is backward: no black pawn beside it is level with it or behind it, and a white pawn attacks the square in front of it.

claims.statement: c6 is Black's only backward pawn.
The square in front of c6 is attacked once by a white pawn (d4).

hints: Backward means: stuck behind its neighbours, with the square in front controlled by an enemy pawn.
Which black pawn has a white pawn attacking the square in front of it?
The d4 pawn attacks c5, the square in front of the pawn on c6.
items.explain: The pawn on c6 has only d5 beside it, and d5 is further advanced, so no neighbour can come up to defend it. White's d4 pawn controls c5, the square in front of it. That makes c6 backward. The a7 pawn is isolated instead (no pawn on the b-file), which is a different weakness.

claims.statement: At depth 16 e4 is within 0.4 pawn of the engine's best move.

After e4 the pawn is attacked three times (d5, Nf6, and the rook on e8 now that the e-file is clear).

hints: Count how often a pawn on e4 would be attacked and how often defended. Look at the e-file too.

items.explain: After e3-e4 the pawn is attacked by the pawn on d5, the knight on f6 and the rook on e8 (the bishop left e7, so the file is clear), and defended by the pawn on f3, the bishop on d3 and the knight on c3. Three against three, and nothing of White's is left loose. After the exchange White has pawns on d4 and e4 while Black's bishop on d6 blocks its own pieces. At depth 16 e4 is the engine's first choice, about 0.4 pawn ahead of the next move.

feedback_by_move.g5f6: Trading on f6 is possible, but it releases the pressure; e4 comes while Black's bishop is badly placed.

items.prompt: Black to move, after ...e5 and the trades. Tap the white pawn that has no white pawn on either neighbouring file (an isolated pawn).

claims.statement: d4 is White's only isolated pawn.
The e-file is open.

hints: Look at the files on both sides of each white pawn.
The c-pawn and the e-pawn have been traded.
Only the pawn on d4 is left alone in the middle.
items.explain: White gave up its c-pawn for Black's d-pawn and later its e-pawn for Black's e-pawn, so the pawn on d4 has no white pawn on c or e. That is an isolated queen pawn. It controls e5 and c5, and it needs pieces to defend it. The e-file is open because neither side has an e-pawn left.

items.prompt: Black to move. We saw ...e5 fail here. Name a preparatory move that keeps the position healthy (several are fine).

items.explain: The knight on d5 and the bishop on c8 are cramped; White's knight on c3 is strong. Nxc3 trades it off. ...b6 develops the bishop, ...Rd8 supports the centre. All three are within 0.4 pawn of the best move at depth 16, while the immediate ...e5 leaves White at least two and a half pawns ahead.
